newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: TENNIS-HINGIS BECOMING TOO HOT TO HANDLE.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-HINGIS BECOMING TOO HOT TO HANDLE.

text.p: Martina Hingis may know how to win but the 16-year-old Swiss has not yet learnt how to lose.
Now the Women's Tennis Association (WTA) is prepared to make sure Hingis does after she indulged in racket-throwing tantrums at the European indoor championship which ended here on Sunday.

In the last eight days, Hingis has won her first career tournament in Filderstadt and reached the European indoor final, confirming her credentials as the undisputed rising star of women's tennis -- and its most temperamental.
At times in both tournaments she displayed the steely composure of a veteran and the petulance of spoilt child.
In a tense semifinal against Germany's Anke Huber at the European indoor on Saturday, Hingis slammed her racket onto the court more then a half-dozen times, kicking it twice.
Like a patient parent, chair umpire Mike Morrissey endured the outbursts until he could ignore them no more, issuing a warning for racket abuse late in the match.
Similar displays followed as she lost Sunday's final to Jana Novotna, with a frustrated Hingis arguing calls and smashing the net.
Even though her on-court tantrums are beginning to occur with alarming regularity, the WTA has been reluctant to punish their protege.
Faced with the eventual retirements of joint world number ones and often-injured Steffi Graf and Monica Seles, the WTA has siezed on Hingis as their future star.

It is also clear the WTA would like Hingis to be a role model after enduring the public relations nightmares that surrounded such teenage talents as American Jennifer Capriati, who became involved in drug abuse and had to leave the sport temporarily.
Cultivating that positive, wholesome image, however, has become increasingly difficult with Hingis regularly storming around the court bouncing rackets off the floor.

"If it keeps on we would be concerned but I think it's something we can deal with now," said Georgina Clark, the WTA European operations director. "We'll be talking to her and it will certainly come up for discussion.
"Sometimes players come up through the ranks not knowing they developed bad habits.
"But when they get here they have to be aware of public relations and what's good for the image of the game.
"We talk to them and explain that they represent and reflect women's tennis."
Hingis dismisses the outbursts as simply a means of keeping her mind on the job.
"When I throw my racket it helps me concentrate," said Hingis. "It's just the way I am. It's better than to keep it inside."
A volatile temperament appears to be part of a Swiss tennis player's make up.

Last January, 1992 Olympic champion Marc Rosset broke his hand in a fit of temper when he smashed it against a sign while playing mixed doubles with Hingis in the finals of the Hopman Cup in Australia.
